subject: Neurology
vignette: A 58-year-old man has a left frontal lobe infarct. He understands speech and can produce meaningless sounds, but he struggles to form words; his speech is slow, labored, and telegraphic. Repetition and writing are also impaired, and he becomes frustrated by his inability to speak.
question: Which cortical region is most likely damaged, given this expressive language deficit?

options.text: Wernicke area in the superior temporal gyrus
Primary auditory cortex in the temporal lobe
Frontal eye field in the middle frontal gyrus
Broca area in the inferior frontal gyrus
Primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe

explanation_correct: Broca area, located in the inferior frontal gyrus (typically the dominant left hemisphere), is the expressive language center. Damage causes Broca (expressive/motor) aphasia: nonfluent, telegraphic speech with relatively preserved comprehension; repetition and writing are impaired, and patients are often aware of and frustrated by the deficit.

explanation_incorrect.A: Wernicke area damage causes receptive aphasia with fluent but meaningless speech and impaired comprehension, the opposite of this patient's presentation.
explanation_incorrect.B: Primary auditory cortex lesions produce hearing or auditory processing deficits, not expressive aphasia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Frontal eye field lesions cause impaired voluntary conjugate gaze, not language deficits.
explanation_incorrect.E: Primary visual cortex lesions cause visual field deficits, not expressive language problems.

educationalObjective: Localize expressive (Broca) aphasia to the inferior frontal gyrus.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 63-year-old woman has a left hemisphere lesion. She speaks fluently with normal cadence, but her speech is filled with nonexistent words and she cannot comprehend spoken or written language. She is unaware of her deficit. A different patient has a lesion that disconnects Broca and Wernicke areas, causing impaired repetition with otherwise intact comprehension and fluent speech.
question: Which region is responsible for the first patient's fluent but meaningless speech with impaired comprehension?

options.text: Broca area in the inferior frontal gyrus
Wernicke area in the superior temporal gyrus
Arcuate fasciculus
Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus)
Angular gyrus

explanation_correct: Wernicke area, in the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, is the receptive language center. Damage produces fluent (Wernicke/receptive) aphasia with impaired comprehension, meaningless speech (word salad and neologisms), and lack of insight. The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke and Broca areas; its isolated lesion causes conduction aphasia with impaired repetition.

explanation_incorrect.A: Broca area damage causes nonfluent expressive aphasia with preserved comprehension, not fluent meaningless speech.
explanation_incorrect.C: The arcuate fasciculus connects Broca and Wernicke areas; its lesion primarily impairs repetition (conduction aphasia) rather than producing fluent meaningless speech with poor comprehension.
explanation_incorrect.D: Primary motor cortex lesions cause weakness, not language comprehension deficits.
explanation_incorrect.E: The angular gyrus is involved in reading, writing, and calculation; its lesion does not classically cause fluent receptive aphasia.

educationalObjective: Localize receptive (Wernicke) aphasia to the superior temporal gyrus and distinguish arcuate fasciculus lesions.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 47-year-old man has a lesion in the middle frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. On examination, he cannot voluntarily turn his eyes to the contralateral side, and his eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion. Reflexive eye movement is preserved.
question: Which cortical area is most likely lesioned, given this gaze abnormality?

options.text: Primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus)
Wernicke area (superior temporal gyrus)
Frontal eye field
Primary visual cortex (occipital lobe)
Broca area (inferior frontal gyrus)

explanation_correct: The frontal eye field, located in the middle frontal gyrus, controls voluntary conjugate eye movements. A unilateral lesion causes inability to voluntarily gaze contralaterally, so the eyes deviate toward the side of the lesion because the intact hemisphere's field drives gaze toward the lesioned side. Reflexive gaze is often preserved.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primary motor cortex lesions cause contralateral weakness, not isolated loss of voluntary conjugate gaze.
explanation_incorrect.B: Wernicke area lesions cause receptive aphasia, not a gaze palsy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Primary visual cortex lesions cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, not gaze deviation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Broca area lesions cause expressive aphasia, not impaired voluntary eye movements.

educationalObjective: Identify the frontal eye field as the cortical center for voluntary conjugate gaze.

subject: Neurology
vignette: A 41-year-old patient sustains a focal cortical injury. The neurology team wants to localize the lesion: the patient has intact primary hearing and vision, and the clinicians review which cortical areas mediate the initial processing of auditory, visual, motor, and somatosensory information.
question: Which of the following correctly pairs a primary cortical function with its anatomically correct location?

options.text: Primary auditory cortex - temporal lobe; primary visual cortex - occipital lobe
Primary auditory cortex - occipital lobe; primary visual cortex - temporal lobe
Primary somatosensory cortex - occipital lobe; primary motor cortex - temporal lobe
Primary visual cortex - parietal lobe; primary auditory cortex - frontal lobe
Primary motor cortex - postcentral gyrus; primary somatosensory cortex - precentral gyrus

explanation_correct: The primary auditory cortex is located in the temporal lobe, and the primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe. The primary motor cortex lies in the precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe, and the primary somatosensory cortex lies in the postcentral gyrus of the parietal lobe. These are classic localization points.

explanation_incorrect.B: This reverses the two: auditory cortex is temporal and visual cortex is occipital.
explanation_incorrect.C: Primary somatosensory cortex is in the parietal (postcentral) region and primary motor cortex is in the frontal (precentral) region, not occipital and temporal.
explanation_incorrect.D: Primary visual cortex is occipital and primary auditory cortex is temporal, not parietal and frontal.
explanation_incorrect.E: This reverses the gyri: motor cortex is precentral and somatosensory cortex is postcentral.

educationalObjective: Match the primary sensory and motor cortices to their correct lobes and gyri.
